headline: High risk of shared-repo write conflicts and medium prompt/cascade risks; no direct evidence of a documented pairwise exploit path.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and edits repo files, and Pipecat can ingest text through shared bus/LLM pipelines. If Aider writes attacker-controlled instructions into shared files or transcripts, Pipecat may treat them as content. The pair lacks direct documented bridging evidence, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Pipecat consumes text from a shared bus or file-backed transcript produced by Aider
IF Aider writes untrusted content into files that Pipecat later parses as instructions
mitigations: Separate Aider and Pipecat into different workspaces
Disable any file-to-agent ingestion path in Pipecat
Add a provenance tag to all Aider-generated files
Require manual review before Pipecat acts on text from Aider
requires-engineering: enforce content-type filtering on the shared bus

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history in a shared repo, while Pipecat handles text, conversation state, and analytics and can call external LLM/STT/TTS services. That creates a plausible path for code or secrets in the workspace to flow into Pipecat outputs or third-party APIs. No direct pair evidence exists, so this remains medium.
conditions: IF the shared repo contains secrets or sensitive source code
IF Pipecat forwards conversation state or file contents to external model providers
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared repo
Use separate credentials for each agent
Disable Pipecat integrations that upload transcripts
Redact sensitive files before either agent reads them
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on shared inputs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider has broad filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and git-state modification in a shared repo; Pipecat runs across shared bus/processes and can also use networked services. Concurrent writes to the same mutable workspace or shared state can corrupt git history or overwrite artifacts. This is a default-dangerous overlap, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or shared working directory
IF Pipecat persists artifacts to the same mutable state that Aider edits
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate checkout
Serialize writes with a lock file
Restrict Aider to read-only mode during Pipecat runs
Snapshot the repo before concurrent sessions
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutual exclusion

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider can generate code or edits that Pipecat may consume as text or workflow input, and Pipecat can then propagate that content through downstream speech or LLM services. The pair does not prove blind trust, but the shared-state design makes unverified handoff plausible. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Pipecat treats Aider output as authoritative without a verification step
IF Aider-generated text is routed into Pipecat actions or prompts
mitigations: Insert a human verification step between agents
Require schema validation on Aider outputs
Log and diff all handoffs before execution
Limit Pipecat to read-only summarization of Aider output
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: Aider is open-source and local repo-focused, while Pipecat is a framework that can route audio/text to many external providers. The main compliance issue is configuration-dependent residency or retention mismatch, not an inherent violation. The pair itself does not show a mandatory breach, so low fits.
conditions: IF Pipecat is configured to send regulated data to non-approved external providers
IF the shared repo contains data subject to stricter retention or residency rules
mitigations: Use only approved providers in Pipecat
Avoid placing regulated data in the shared repo
Document retention settings for each provider
Turn off analytics for sensitive sessions
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing by data class
